column5: name exalted above all blessing and praise
column6: The commentary keeps the name itself as the object to be raised; Nehemiah’s public prayer blesses God’s glorious name, exalted above blessing and praise, an unusually close liturgical formulation.

column5: no one like YHWH, whose name is great in might
column6: The commentary joins the highest title to the absence of any namesake or rival; Jeremiah says there is none like YHWH and that his name is great in might, joining uniqueness, name, and power.

column5: glory due to the name
column6: The commentary distinguishes praising the name itself from acting by means of it; this psalm tells worshipers to ascribe to YHWH the glory due his name and to bring an offering.

column5: worship in holy splendor
column6: The commentary makes tasbih an enacted practice as well as a judgment; the next line of the psalm calls the earth to bow before YHWH in holy splendor, joining name-praise to bodily worship.

column5: praising the great and awesome name
column6: The commentary says the name is to be guarded and held high; this psalm commands praise of YHWH’s great and awesome name and immediately calls him holy.

column5: the name great among nations with pure offerings
column6: The commentary asks that the name be kept from false attribution; Malachi says YHWH’s name is great among the nations and associates it with pure offerings from sunrise to sunset, extending the name’s honor beyond one people.

column5: the Lord enthroned high and lifted up
column6: The commentary preserves the reading of al-aʿlā as the Lord himself being highest; Isaiah’s vision places the Lord on a high and lofty throne as a prophet receives a commission.

column5: the thrice-holy proclamation
column6: The commentary presents tasbih as declaring God free of defect; the seraphim call one to another “Holy, holy, holy” and fill the scene with God’s glory, a foundational Jewish liturgical formula of divine holiness.

column5: morning stars singing at creation
column6: The commentary notes stars moving in their courses alongside the praise of creation; Job’s creation scene pictures morning stars singing together, making celestial praise explicit.

column5: do not invoke the names of other gods
column6: The commentary warns against assigning divine naming to rivals; Exodus tells Israel not even to mention the names of other gods, a concrete discipline of exclusive worship.

column5: Moses says he is slow of speech
column6: The commentary recalls Moses asking God to open his chest and make his mission easy; Exodus has Moses object that he is not eloquent and is slow of speech, a shared commissioning problem stated differently.

column5: Aaron is appointed to meet Moses
column6: The commentary says Moses asks that his brother share the task so they can praise God; Exodus has God appoint Aaron, already on his way to meet Moses, as the brother who will speak with him.

column5: Aaron speaks while Moses is as God
column6: The commentary links a single messenger, his brother’s aid, and a divine mission; Exodus says Aaron will be Moses’ mouth and Moses will be as God to him, clarifying delegated speech without the Qur’anic stated purpose of praise.

column5: the name that answers is declared God
column6: The commentary contrasts the one true Lord with names humans assign to rivals; Elijah proposes a public test in which each side calls its god by name and the one who answers by fire is God.

column5: Baal’s name is called without an answer
column6: The commentary calls idolatrous names unsupported names; the prophets of Baal invoke their god from morning until noon, but no voice answers, giving that critique a concrete narrative scene.

column5: Elijah invokes YHWH’s name before Israel
column6: The commentary links praise of the name with a messenger’s public task; Elijah prays that the people will know YHWH is God and that he acted at YHWH’s word, making the name known through the sign.

column5: Israel confesses YHWH alone is God
column6: The commentary says divine lordship must not be distributed among rivals; after the fire, the people fall down and confess that YHWH is God, the scene’s explicit verdict on the competing names.

column5: Cain receives a protective mark
column6: The commentary develops a possible Arabic name-as-brand image but does not claim a Hebrew cognate; God marks Cain so others will recognize and spare him, adding protection to the mark’s identifying function.

column5: God gives Abram the name Abraham
column6: The commentary says a name raises and distinguishes its bearer; God renames Abram Abraham and explains the name by his future role as father of many nations, showing identity conferred by God.

column5: knowledge of YHWH compared with dawn and rain
column6: The commentary brings the first rain, green pasture, and the knowledge of God into one hearing; Hosea says let us know YHWH, whose coming is like dawn and like rain watering the land, a particularly close meeting of knowledge and agricultural renewal.

column5: YHWH is righteous, while the speaker rebelled
column6: The commentary says Jonah’s tasbih assigns perfection to God and wrongdoing to himself; Lamentations says YHWH is in the right while the speaker has rebelled, a direct ethical form of that reversal.

column5: stars and natural powers mistaken for gods
column6: The commentary distinguishes celestial motion from the Creator and rejects names placed on created things; Wisdom lists sun, moon, stars, and other natural powers as things people mistakenly treated as gods.

column5: creation’s greatness points to its Maker
column6: The commentary places the sky, stars, rain, and pasture under one sustaining Lord; Wisdom argues that the greatness and beauty of created things allow their Maker to be perceived, sharpening the distinction between sign and source.

column5: a good name rises above other crowns
column6: The commentary develops name as elevation and public distinction; this saying places the crown of a good name above kingship, priesthood, and Torah, giving Jewish ethical use to the image of a name raised above.

column5: the Lord’s Prayer recited three times each day
column6: The commentary joins tasbih to repeated prayer and embodied practice; the Didache instructs Christians to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times daily, turning its hallowing of the name into a regular liturgical act.

column5: Psalm 2’s royal “son” applied to Jesus
column6: The commentary rejects divine offspring; Hebrews quotes the royal son formula from Psalm 2 as speech about the Son, showing how Christian interpretation makes that Hebrew royal language christological.

column5: Israel called God’s firstborn son
column6: The commentary rejects God having a child; Exodus calls Israel God’s firstborn in a covenant demand to Pharaoh, showing that biblical son language can name a people’s relation to God rather than biological offspring.

column5: the lawless one exalts himself as God
column6: The commentary sets Pharaoh’s “I am your highest lord” against rightful divine sovereignty; Paul describes an end-time figure who exalts himself above every object of worship and proclaims himself God, a close later counter-image.

column5: the beast blasphemes God’s name
column6: The commentary says tasbih separates God from false claims about him; Revelation’s beast opens its mouth to blaspheme God’s name, giving a Christian apocalyptic image of the name’s profanation.

column5: seeing God’s face with his name on foreheads
column6: The commentary brings the divine face and a bodily name-mark into its reading; Revelation joins the two directly: the servants see God’s face and bear his name on their foreheads.

column5: one baptismal name over Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
column6: The commentary says different names belong to one possessor; Matthew gives baptism in the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a Christian formula that keeps unity while adding a distinct triune account.

column5: one king and one name over all the earth
column6: The commentary holds the highest Lord’s name apart from competing claims; Zechariah says YHWH will be king over all the earth and his name one, joining universal rule to exclusive naming.

column5: YHWH’s name and renown endure through generations
column6: The commentary contrasts the enduring highest name with fading life; this psalm says YHWH’s name and renown endure through all generations, extending the name’s permanence beyond an individual lifetime.

column5: YHWH’s name as a strong tower of refuge
column6: The commentary describes a name as a raised sign that protects and identifies its bearer; Proverbs says the name of YHWH is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are safe, making refuge part of the name’s force.
